A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FreeFuse. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, with retained material identifiable despite renumbering and substantial layout changes.

before.justification: v2 reports original generation benchmarks, component ablations, attention-localization measurements, user preferences, and latency results, including experiments in Appendices A, E, and F.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds perturbation measurements, a quantitative mask-extraction sweep, a router ablation, and the evaluations in Appendices E and F.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1 and 3.3 generalize routing from one subject-specific LoRA per region to semantic groups containing multiple adapters, including identity/attribute combinations and shared style adapters. This extends the routing rule while retaining FreeFuseAttn, mask post-processing, and the two-stage inference framework.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation using LoRAShop's public real-person LoRA and prompt data in Appendix F, and uses its LoRA collection for perturbation analysis. The heterogeneous 15-LoRA benchmark and existing SDXL/Illustrious-XL coverage remain, so this is a limited coverage extension.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds a comparison variant with the Router removed but attention bias retained. The five external baselines in Table 1 and the SDXL comparator set remain unchanged; Table 6 reuses the existing external method families under the public protocol.

E3.justification: v3 substantially expands evaluation design through a 300-sample step/block sweep using Precision@10%, a bias-only control, controlled quality comparisons at 2–5 LoRAs, and the public dual-subject protocol with CLIP-T bigG and Aesthetic v2. The existing 470-image main benchmark and previously stated inference settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether early blocks carry weaker LoRA perturbations, quantitatively validate the previously selected extraction step/block, isolate routing from attention bias, and measure quality as LoRA count increases (Figures 4, 6, and 17; Tables 2 and 5). These substantially strengthen the mechanistic and sensitivity evidence beyond v2's retained analyses.

E5.justification: New Figure 4 reports explicit 95% confidence intervals for the perturbation ratios: 1.80 with [1.56, 2.02], and 2.67 with [1.92, 3.26]. This adds uncertainty reporting, but v3 does not specify their construction or establish an increase in repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Table 1, retained Table 2 rows, and latency values are unchanged. Substantial additions include the bias-only ArcFace score of 0.2669 versus 0.4275 for full FreeFuse, the mask-sweep peak of 0.704, perturbation measurements, and Tables 5–6. Under the new public protocol, FreeFuse leads ArcFace and CLIP-T bigG, but its Aesthetic v2 score of 5.7426 is lowest among the six methods.

T1.justification: Equation 1 is generalized to sum residuals over semantic groups and their adapter sets. Section 3.1 also withdraws the inference that attention locality makes cross-region perturbations mathematically negligible and guarantees uncontaminated synthesis. The remaining attention and post-processing mathematics is substantially retained; no new theorem or proof replaces that inference.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion substantially narrow the central mechanism claim: v2 describes sufficient conflict mitigation and elimination of leakage, whereas v3 claims empirically supported suppression of direct LoRA interference while preserving global context propagation. The introduction also broadens routing support to multiple adapters per semantic group. The training-free framework and principal performance claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the complete-isolation interpretation with an explicit distinction between direct residual injection and indirect propagation through base attention. New perturbation measurements support an explanation based on weak early-block residuals and stronger, more localized deeper effects. Appendix A adopts the same qualification, while the computational-overhead and future-video discussion remains essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 supplies important missing details: 10% anchor selection, temperature 4000, exact FLUX blocks and projection branches receiving routing, and restarting Phase 2 from the same latent. Appendix G newly discloses 17 participants, ages 18–40, 40 cases, and ranking averaging. These are disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to existing settings. The abstract also replaces the direct code link with a project-page link.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive related-work positioning remain unchanged. Section 2 retains the same contrasts with retraining, external segmentation, and other generation approaches. Expanded author names and revised bibliography formatting do not introduce new research references.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted rewrites to the abstract, mechanism discussion, and conclusion, expands technical explanations, fixes the missing Momentum Averaging item heading, and adds acknowledgments and two appendix sections. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain, rather than undergoing wholesale narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: v3 adopts TMLR typography, headers, author formatting, and page layout. It adds Figures 4, 6, and 17 and Tables 5–6, expands the ablation and hyperparameter tables, and redisplays existing latency results in main-text Table 3. Earlier Figure 3 becomes Figure 5 with replaced examples; most existing galleries and appendix figures are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the paper's justification and reproducibility. It replaces v2's mathematical-negligibility claim with a qualified empirical account supported by perturbation measurements and a direct router ablation, while supplying important implementation and user-study details. The public evaluation adds useful independent evidence despite revealing an aesthetic-score disadvantage. Unchanged main scores and incomplete confidence-interval documentation limit the gains, but do not outweigh these substantial improvements.
